Photograph: Tierney L Cross/Bloomberg via Getty Images US military Pentagon official overseeing military AI sold millions worth of stock in AI firm Exclusive: financial disclosures from Emil Michael – who also reaped millions from xAI stock earlier this year – show he sold his Perplexity stock for up to $25m Aram Roston Tue 1 Sep 2026 15.17 EDT Last modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 15.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The top Pentagon official overseeing military artificial intelligence policy, who reaped profits earlier this year of up to $24m selling his private investment in Elon Musk’s AI company, has now sold his holdings in another AI company for between $5m and $25m, according to records seen by the Guardian. (Federal financial records show ranges of dollar values rather than specific figures.) Earlier this year, the Guardian disclosed that the official, Emil Michael, had profited handsomely from his investment in Musk’s xAI in January, with a gain of between 400% and 4,800% . Michael’s latest financial disclosures show that in June, he sold off his shares in Perplexity, an AI-powered search engine. Recent reports have said Perplexity is looking for a financial valuation of $30bn. The records don’t reveal whether he made a profit on the sale because of the large dollar range listed in his disclosures. The Lever reported in March that Michael had the holdings in Perplexity. His financial disclosure filings from 2025 also show that he had received a personal loan from Perplexity a year earlier, of between $250,000 and $500,000, at an interest rate of 4.57%. He also joined a Perplexity advisory board, but his disclosures said he stepped down upon entering federal service. Some of his Perplexity stock was vested and some was unvested, and in his ethics agreement he pledged not to make a profit off the unvested stock. It is not clear from the disclosures what stock he sold. Perplexity announced a contract with the US government’s General Services Administration in November of last year, though records do not show specific ties to the Pentagon. “He should have sold all interest in the company before he started working,” said ethics expert Richard Painter, a former lawyer at the White House under George W Bush. “That’s the way we would have done it back when I was working for president.” A Pentagon spokesperson said Michael and other defense officials “are in full compliance with ethics laws and regulations. Any claims otherwise are false”. The spokesperson said the department has “a rigorous, multi-layered ethics framework”. Painter said Michael’s ownership in an AI company would not be a violation of law but would have raised questions because of appearances. “Most administrations would have said get out of that stock before you start that job.” Michael’s lucrative trading while at the Pentagon isn’t limited to AI companies. His latest disclosure also shows he has now realized gains at least 473% selling holdings he owned in a separate non-public company. According to the records, Michael sold holdings in Brex LLC in April for at least $5m. Brex, a financial software company, is backed by Peter Thiel and was acquired by Capitol One that month. Michael had been a consultant at the firm. Though the firm was privately held and stock prices were not available, Michael’s holdings jumped during his time in government: he reported in March 2025 that his Brex holdings were worth just a maximum of $750,000. Michael’s profit in the Brex sale could have been as large as $24m or as little as $4.25m. Brex, unlike Musk’s xAI, does not appear to do any reported work with the US government. Michael was the face of the department’s war against AI company Anthropic. He is a frequent guest on podcasts, including on the tech podcast called Sourcery – and the episode on which he appeared in December, was sponsored by Brex, while Michael was still an investor in the company. It was called “Misunderstood Power: Emil Michael on the Truth about DOW and Defense Tech.” Emil was chief business officer at Uber from 2014 to 2017. BuzzFeedNews reported in 2014 that Michael had privately floated digging up dirt on critical journalists, though Michael said the comment, at what he thought was an off-the-record dinner, didn’t reflect his views. Photograph: Oleg Kozhemyako/Reuters View image in fullscreen Trucks drive along a road during a ceremony for the opening the first road bridge between Russia and North Korea across the Tumen River. Photograph: Oleg Kozhemyako/Reuters Russia Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared border Connection across Tumen River is further sign of closer ties between the two countries since start of war in Ukraine Pjotr Sauer Mon 7 Sep 2026 05.53 EDT Last modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 06.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia and North Korea have opened the first road bridge across their shared border , in the latest sign of the rapidly deepening ties between the two countries since the start of the war in Ukraine. The one-kilometre bridge spans the Tumen River between Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea , along a remote and sparsely populated stretch of the countries’ shared border just a few miles from the coast. Speaking by video link during the bridge’s opening ceremony on Monday, Russia’s prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, said the new crossing would spur development in a range of areas, including tourism, while creating new jobs “I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” Mishustin said. Russia and North Korea finalising first road crossing amid concerns it serves as Ukraine war supply route Read more The road bridge is named after the Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korea’s founding leader, Kim Il-sung, from an assassination attempt by a pro-South Korean group. View image in fullscreen A newly built bridge connects Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea. Photograph: Ministry of Transport of the Russian Federation After the opening ceremony, convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge from both sides. Russia and the secretive North Korea regime are already connected by a railway bridge across the Tumen, as well as regular flights between Vladivostok and Pyongyang. Ukrainian human rights groups have warned that the bridge may be intended to provide a discreet military logistics corridor between the two countries. Truth Hounds, a Ukrainian human rights organisation, has described it as a likely future corridor for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, while allowing Russian technology and resources to travel in the opposite direction with less risk of detection. Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened dramatically since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea has sent thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help Moscow repel a Ukrainian incursion launched there in 2024. From ammunition to ballistic missiles: how North Korea arms Russia in the Ukraine war Read more In return, Russia is believed to have provided North Korea with air-defence missiles, electronic warfare equipment, drones and spy-satellite technology, according to South Korean intelligence. Russian and North Korean officials have also touted North Korea as a new holiday destination since the country reopened to Russian tourists in 2024, with thousands of Russians visiting its newly opened beach resorts and ski slopes since then. Russia’s increasingly close embrace of totalitarian North Korea has raised eyebrows even in Moscow. During an interview with the Russian broadcaster RBC last month, a reporter asked Sergei Lavrov, Russia’s longtime foreign minister, how the country had “ended up” with just “two allies – North Korea and Iran”. Lavrov pushed back against the premise, saying there was “nothing wrong” with such company. At the same time, some of Russia’s traditional partners have shown growing frustration with Moscow’s continuing war in Ukraine and the fallout it has caused across the region. During a meeting in July, Kazakhstan’s president, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, a longtime ally of Moscow, told the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, that he was hearing from leaders of many countries who questioned why Russia was still waging the war. “The nature of the conflict isn’t entirely clear for many, including us,” Tokayev told Putin. https://www.baltictimes.com/niittyla_kan.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Niittyla&Kanto's Alex Kanto: 'AI is reshaping B2B sales across the Baltics and Nordics' 2026-09-21 Linas Jegelevicius For companies in the Baltics, international expansion is often a necessity rather than a choice. Small domestic markets mean businesses in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania must look abroad relatively early, but building dedicated sales teams in every new market can be expensive. Alex Kanto, partner at Finnish B2B sales and go-to-market company Niittyla&Kanto Oy, believes AI-assisted research, preparation and outbound sales workflows can make that expansion faster, more targeted and more cost-efficient. “Rather than using AI simply to generate greater volumes of automated outreach, we use it to improve the quality of the outreach we already do. AI-assisted research and preparation help us understand potential customers faster, filter out irrelevant accounts and focus human effort on prospects with genuine commercial potential. Clients do not buy our service because of AI; they buy the results that better efficiency and quality can produce. Niittyla&Kanto already works with clients across Finland and the Baltics, and I myself live in Tallinn. We increasingly think about the business on a Baltic-Nordic level,” Alex Kanto told The Baltic Times. How did Niittyla&Kanto start, and what gap in the B2B sales market did you originally set out to fill? My co-founder and I met at school and later worked together in a few different sales roles during Covid-19. Through that experience, we saw a gap in B2B appointment setting: there was plenty of volume-based cold calling, but much less focus on combining good targeting, relevant messaging and different outreach channels. One of our first projects at N&K was actually international appointment setting for an EdTech company expanding around the world. That taught us very early how different cross-border sales is from simply working through a local call list. From there, we first scaled the model in Finland, but today one of the most valuable things we can bring to a client is cross-border go-to-market support. We can help a client identify a new market, find the right companies and decision-makers to contact, test how their value proposition resonates and start building the first qualified sales conversations there. What exactly do you do for a client, and where does your role typically end? Niittyla&Kanto provides B2B appointment setting, outbound sales and go-to-market support for companies expanding across Finland, the Baltics, the Nordics and wider international markets. Depending on the client, that can include B2B market research, target-account selection, decision-maker research, lead generation, outbound prospecting and multichannel sales outreach through email, LinkedIn, phone and other relevant channels. For companies entering a new market, we can essentially operate as an outsourced sales development resource: helping validate the market, build the initial pipeline and book qualified B2B sales meetings before the company commits to building a full local sales organisation. Our job is to create the right commercial conversations. Once a qualified meeting is booked with a prospect who has genuine relevance, the client's own sales team normally takes over the opportunity and closing process. The same model works in both directions: we help Baltic companies with international market entry and customer acquisition, while also helping Nordic and other international companies enter Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Finland. What does the business look like today, and what are your targets for the next three to five years? We are intentionally still a founder-led team, and I think that is increasingly an advantage rather than something we need to grow out of. Over the years, we have sold well over €1 million worth of appointment setting and outbound sales services. More importantly, that work has helped create tens of millions of euros in sales pipeline and commercial opportunities for our customers across a very broad range of industries and markets. That repetition has given us a fairly specialised understanding of one part of the sales cycle: how you identify the right commercial opportunities and turn a cold market into actual conversations. Earlier, we thought scaling a service company mainly meant adding more people. Today we think much more about scaling the process and giving a smaller number of capable people better tools, data and workflows. Over the next few years, the goal is to build N&K into an increasingly international sales partner, particularly for companies that need a cost-efficient way to establish themselves in a new market before investing heavily in local sales infrastructure. What types of companies and industries make up your customer base? Are you increasingly looking beyond Finland? We've worked with companies ranging from SaaS and professional services to industrial technology, energy, healthcare technology and enterprise consulting. Technology and SaaS companies are a particularly natural fit because they often have strong products but relatively limited sales resources, and their addressable market is usually international from the beginning. We already work with clients in the Baltics as well as Finland, and I live in Tallinn myself. So I don't really view Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania as some future export project for us. We already operate from this region and increasingly think about the business on a Baltic-Nordic level. For Baltic companies in particular, international sales is almost built into the equation. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are excellent places to build companies, but the domestic markets are small. If you want to build something significant, you usually have to learn how to compete cross-border relatively early. That is exactly the type of problem where our experience can be useful. How are AI and automation changing your business? AI has become an extremely useful tool for us, but people don't buy our service because it uses AI. They buy it because they want qualified sales opportunities, better market coverage and ultimately new customers. That distinction is important to us. The fundamentals of good B2B sales haven't changed. You still need the right company, the right person, the right context and a reason for them to care. AI simply allows us to do parts of that work much more efficiently and, in many cases, at a higher level of quality. Research is a good example. We can now analyse much more information about a company and its commercial situation before approaching it. That helps us filter out companies where there is no meaningful context and spend more time on the ones where there is. Ironically, one of the biggest benefits of AI for us has therefore been the ability to contact fewer companies, not more. There is already enough AI-generated noise in everyone's inbox. If the only thing AI enables is sending more generic outreach faster, it is being used badly. For a service company like ours, the interesting part is that AI can improve both efficiency and quality at the same time. That changes the economics of the service. Work that previously required a much larger amount of manual preparation can be delivered more efficiently, which allows us to make high-quality outbound and go-to-market support accessible and commercially useful to smaller companies as well. The customer doesn't need to care which AI model or workflow is behind that. They should care that the service is relevant, cost-efficient and produces results. Could AI eventually replace some work currently performed by sales professionals? Certainly. A lot of manual list work, research, CRM administration, data entry and repetitive preparation will probably disappear or become heavily automated. But I see that more as a change in where human time is valuable. A good salesperson should not spend most of the day copying information between systems or manually researching basic company information. They should understand customers, make decisions, build trust and have commercial conversations. AI is a bit like what Excel became for finance or what search engines became for knowledge work. Neither removed the underlying profession, but eventually it became difficult to imagine a high-performing professional choosing not to use them. I think AI is heading in the same direction. Today it can still feel like an advantage. Eventually, it will simply be part of the expected toolkit. And again, the customer is unlikely to buy something simply because AI is involved. AI has to translate into something tangible: better quality, lower cost, faster delivery or a better result. Otherwise, it is just technology for technology's sake. Do you see opportunities to expand into Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania? We already have clients in the Baltics, and because I live in Tallinn, I see the region as part of our home market rather than simply an expansion target. What is especially interesting is helping Baltic companies go the other direction. A company can build an excellent product in Tallinn, Riga or Vilnius, but at some point it needs customers in Stockholm, Helsinki, London, Germany or the US. Building a sales organisation in every market before knowing what works is expensive. A cross-border go-to-market partner can help bridge that gap: map the market, identify the relevant accounts and decision-makers, localise the commercial approach, generate qualified B2B leads and meetings, and collect real market feedback. The same applies to a Finnish or international company entering the Baltics. The fundamentals of sales travel well, but the approach still needs to respect the market, buyer behaviour and context. What is the biggest obstacle to scaling Niittyla&Kanto? Maintaining quality while increasing reach. Appointment setting looks simple from the outside, but doing it well requires quite a lot of judgement. You are representing another company's brand in what may be its first interaction with a future customer. AI-assisted research and workflow automation allow us to make preparation and execution much more efficient, but efficiency only matters if the quality stays high or improves. We don't want to automate the customer or prospect out of the process. So the challenge is building something that becomes more scalable and accessible without becoming more generic. That's also why I like the founder-led model. Decisions about quality, customers and how we represent them remain very close to the people who have the most at stake in the company. Where do you see the company in five years? I think AI itself will become much less of a differentiator and much more like standard business infrastructure. Twenty years ago, having a good website or CRM could itself be a competitive advantage. Today nobody describes themselves as a "website-enabled company" because those tools have simply become part of doing business. I suspect AI will follow a similar path. For N&K, the goal isn't to become an AI company. It is to become a better international sales and go-to-market company by using whatever technology gives our clients an advantage. People won't buy from us in five years because we use AI any more than they buy from a company today because its employees use Outlook or Google. They will buy if we can produce the outcome they need at the right quality and cost. Five years from now, I would like us to be a recognised cross-border B2B sales partner between the Baltics, the Nordics and wider international markets, particularly for companies that want to test, enter and establish themselves in a new market without immediately building a large local sales organisation. The tools behind that service will certainly change. The underlying job probably won't: find the right commercial opportunities and turn them into conversations. https://hvg.hu/cegauto/20261112_visszate.text: Az új részben is van minden, amiért annak idején nézettek lettek az epizódok. Hosszabb kihagyás után újraindult a rendőrség videós sorozata, a Pofátlan(tan)ítás . A 2.0 kiegészítő címkét kapta, és ismét a közlekedési szabályokat látványosan megszegő autósokat veszi célba. A sorozat 2019-ben indult, és hamar nagyon nézetté váltak ezek a videók. A rendőrök civilnek látszó, fedélzeti kamerákkal felszerelt autókból figyelték a forgalmat, majd a kirívó szabálytalanságokat elkövető sofőröket azonnal megállították, illetve a hozzájuk eljutott videók alapján indítottak eljárásokat. Az új sorozatban ismét azonnali intézkedések láthatók, a szabályszegésekhez pedig a büntetési tételeket is feltüntetik. Ezúttal nemcsak autóst, hanem kerékpárost is felelősségre vontak. Keménydiszkontosodik az Aldi és ezt szebben becsomagolva hivatalosan is bejelentette. Megkérdeztük a vásárlókat, hogyan látják a változó üzleteket.
